appraisal_events.evidence: Oriane's audacious quip to the grand-duke about Tolstoy scandalizes the Courvoisier but 'émerveillait les Guermantes'; retold by the comtesse d'Argencourt as proof Oriane is 'fine comme l'ambre, maligne comme un singe, douée pour tout,' literary admirers who will never meet her imagine her as more marvelous than 'la princesse Badroul Boudour' and feel their own convictions fortified merely because so noble a person shares them.
appraisal_events.explanation: Oriane's wit and rank combine, through circulating gossip and flattering retellings, to inflate her reputation into near-legendary status among both her own clan and literary hangers-on who barely know her.

appraisal_events.evidence: Mme de Villeparisis, who has endless raillery for her own nephew the prince de Guermantes over his obsession with birth, nonetheless sees the mysterious 'Génie de la famille,' not the family's professed creed that only intelligence, heart, and talent matter, settle Oriane's marriage on 'l'homme le plus riche et le mieux né... le prince des Laumes.'
appraisal_events.explanation: The passage exposes a stark gap between Oriane's and Mme de Villeparisis's proclaimed anti-snobbish values and the wholly conventional, rank-and-wealth-driven marriage that actually results, diminishing the sincerity of their professed principles.

appraisal_events.evidence: Saint-Loup's devotion to Rachel, for all the horror it caused his family, 'comportait... moins de mensonge que celui des demoiselles Guermantes en général,' who preach intellectual equality yet always end by marrying a wealthy duke; Saint-Loup 'agissait... conformément à ses théories, ce qui faisait dire qu'il était dans une mauvaise voie.'
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator credits Saint-Loup with more genuine consistency between his professed values and his actions than the Guermantes women show, even as that very consistency earns him social condemnation as being on a bad path.

status_effects.explanation: Her reputation for wit and rank is amplified through spreading gossip and public retellings into something close to legend, witnessed by her clan's admiration and literary hangers-on.
Her professed indifference to rank and wealth is undercut when the actual choice of husband is driven entirely by birth and fortune.
Her mockery of others for caring about birth sits uneasily against her own role in steering her niece toward the richest, best-born match available.
The narrator judges him more sincere and consistent than the Guermantes women, who preach equality but practice conventional ambition.
His family and society explicitly regard his devotion to Rachel as putting him on a disreputable path, a witnessed social judgment against him.

ambiguities: The narrator's account of Oriane's growing legend (E1) blends genuine wit with a satirized, credulous hero-worship among literary admirers, complicating how purely positive this elevation should be read.
